message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of tasks:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from operating system tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel processing – originally built to render graphics, now also used for scientific computing, machine learning, etc. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32) optimized for low latency, complex control flow, and high single‑thread performance. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores optimized for throughput; each core can execute the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously (SIMD). |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex instruction set architecture (CISC) with sophisticated branch prediction, out‑of‑order execution, and large caches. | Reduced instruction set architecture (RISC) with many identical pipelines; focuses on executing the same operation over many data points. |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, deep memory hierarchy, and sophisticated prefetching. | Smaller per‑core cache, relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR) and shared memory across many cores. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Serial or lightly parallel tasks, branching logic, I/O, OS services. | Data‑parallel workloads: matrix multiplications, image/video processing, neural network inference/training, scientific simulations. |
| **Performance Metrics** | Clock speed (GHz), instructions per cycle (IPC), single‑thread performance. | FLOPS (floating‑point operations per second), memory bandwidth, throughput for many small tasks. |
| **Energy Efficiency** | Optimized for power‑constrained devices (mobile CPUs) and high performance in desktops/servers. | Designed for massive parallelism; can consume more power overall but delivers higher throughput per watt for suitable workloads. |

In short, a CPU excels at handling diverse, sequential tasks quickly, while a GPU shines when you need to perform the same operation on a huge number of data items simultaneously. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU manages general tasks and orchestrates the GPU, which does the heavy lifting for graphics rendering or parallel computations.
